This island paradise promises an extraordinary safari. Madagascar is one of the most biodiverse countries on Earth, home to thousands of species of plant and animal life of which about 80% cannot be found anywhere else on the planet. Turquoise seas, silky sands and a wide array of endemic creatures, including lemurs, fossas, chameleons, and bizarre insects that seem plucked from fantasy. Fascinating Malagasy culture, vibrant cuisine and iconic baobabs… this is an island worth experiencing.

For travellers seeking a safari beyond the ordinary, Madagascar delivers natural marvels at every turn while supporting critical conservation efforts for some of the planet's most endangered ecosystems.

One of the last of his kind. His tusks sweep so low they almost graze the ground – a natural wonder so rare that fewer than 100 elephants like him are thought to remain across all of Africa. At least eight of them call Tsavo home. KM2 was first identified as a tusker in August 2015, though he had been spotted many times before from the air. He's recognisable by his clean right ear, a tear in his left, and scars along his lower right flank. We've partnered with Tsavo Trust, who monitor and conserve the elephant populations of Tsavo Conservation Area, with a specific focus on protecting its tuskers. Their aerial and ground teams work tirelessly to keep elephants like KM2 alive in a world that still threatens them, from poachers targeting ivory to trophy hunters actively seeking out tuskers beyond Kenya's borders. These magnificent elephants need people in their corner. Groundbreaking research in Tanzania has revealed that leopards can be identified by their roars – with 93% accuracy. Just as every leopard has distinctive rosette patterns, each has a unique vocalisation that researchers can now use to track these elusive cats non-invasively. This innovative conservation tool comes at a critical time. Leopard numbers are declining, they're listed as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, and in places like Hoedspruit, South Africa, seven leopards were killed on roads in 2024 alone. From bioacoustic monitoring in Tanzania to road ecology projects protecting leopards in the Lowveld, researchers are finding new ways to conserve these masters of stealth.
